what: SM Energy drills for oil and natural gas in Texas and Utah. Its core areas are the Midland Basin in West Texas, the Austin Chalk and Eagle Ford in South Texas, and the Uinta Basin in Utah.
customers: Refiners, midstream companies and commodity traders. Prices are set by the market.
money: Crude from the Midland, Austin Chalk and Uinta basins.
Associated gas and liquids produced alongside the oil.
moat: Large contiguous acreage positions in basins where SM has drilled for years, which means it knows how each rock interval behaves. The Uinta Basin position, added recently, is less contested than the Permian and offers lower acquisition cost per acre.
risks: Oil prices determine everything, and revenue has been volatile: $3.4B in 2022, $2.4B in 2023, $3.2B in 2025.
Shale wells decline quickly, so much of the cash flow must be reinvested every year merely to maintain production.
Debt rose to about $2.9B against $368.0M of cash after the Uinta acquisition.
Uinta crude is waxy and has to be heated to move, which limits which refineries can take it and widens the price discount.
Drilling and service costs rise when activity picks up, squeezing margins just as prices improve.
opportunities: The shares trade at about 6.4 times earnings and 3.6 times EV/EBITDA, among the lowest multiples in the sector.
Free cash flow of roughly $1.1B against a $6.9B market value is a very large yield.
Eighteen analysts average a $44.33 target, roughly 51% above the current price.
The Uinta acreage extends the drilling inventory by years, which addresses the main criticism of mid-sized shale producers.
watch: Free cash flow after the Uinta debt is paid down. The producer is cheap because of the leverage it took on; deleveraging is what would close the valuation gap.
